A · Designed Features → Learned Ones Key Terms — The Smallest Unit

Neuron

/ˈnjʊə.rɒn/

One number out of many numbers in: multiply each input by a weight, add them and a bias, then pass through an activation.

หน่วยเดียวที่รับหลายค่าแล้วให้ค่าเดียว — คูณน้ำหนัก บวก bias แล้วผ่าน activation

Weights and bias

/weɪts/

The numbers being learned. Everything a trained model "knows" is a list of these.

ตัวเลขที่โมเดลเรียน · ทุกอย่างที่โมเดลรู้คือลิสต์ของตัวเลขพวกนี้

Activation (ReLU)

/ˌæk.tɪˈveɪ.ʃən/

A simple bend applied after the sum: max(0,x). Without it, depth buys nothing at all.

ฟังก์ชันหักงอที่ใส่หลังการบวก · max(0, x) · ถ้าไม่มี ต่อให้ซ้อนกี่ชั้นก็ไม่ได้อะไรเพิ่ม

Layer

/ˈleɪ.ər/

Many neurons looking at the same input at once. Stack layers and each one sees what the previous one produced.

กลุ่ม neuron ที่มองข้อมูลชุดเดียวกันพร้อมกัน · ซ้อนเป็นชั้น ๆ ชั้นถัดไปเห็นผลของชั้นก่อน

🔑

Nothing in that list is complicated on its own. A neural network is a very large number of very small arithmetic steps — the difficulty is never one neuron, it is bookkeeping at scale.

1 / 63
A · Designed Features → Learned Ones One neuron, in full
y=max(0,∑i​wi​xi​+b)

Three steps and no more: multiply each input by its own weight, add everything up plus a bias, bend the result at zero.

Compare it with a pixel's worth of convolution from Session 2:
y=∑k​hk​xk​ — the same weighted sum. A neuron just adds a bias and a bend.

1 / 63
A · Designed Features → Learned Ones Without the bend, depth buys you nothing
📐

A weighted sum of weighted sums is still a weighted sum — the middle panel is a straight line no matter how many layers you stack. The activation is the only thing that makes a second layer worth having, and ReLU is the one almost everyone uses: it is one comparison per number, and it does not squash large values the way sigmoid does.

1 / 63
A · Designed Features → Learned Ones What eight hidden neurons can do that a line cannot
🎯

50.0% against 100.0% — and 50% is what you get by guessing. The straight line is not badly tuned; no straight line exists that separates a ring from its centre. Eight ReLU units bend the space until one does. Everything deeper is more of this.

1 / 63
A · Designed Features → Learned Ones 🌍 Use case: what changed in 2012, and what did not

🧑‍🔬

Before

A PhD's worth of work went into designing one descriptor — SIFT in 2004, HOG in 2005. Each new problem needed a new descriptor and a new expert.

📈

The shift

Once there were a million labelled images and a GPU to run them through, letting the model find its own features beat every hand-designed pipeline on ImageNet.

🧰

What did not change

The operation. A CNN's first layer computes edge responses — the same thing you wrote by hand in Session 2 — because that is what is useful.

⚖️

Keep the hook's number in mind while you hear this: on a small, clean, low-resolution task, the designed features lost by under two points. The case for learning them is not that it always wins by a lot — it is that it scales to problems nobody knows how to design a descriptor for.

1 / 63
A · Designed Features → Learned Ones ↩ So why did the field abandon them?

Not because they were bad. Because designing one costs a person, and learning one costs data — and data got cheap while experts did not.

HOG counts edge directions because Dalal and Triggs decided pedestrians show up in edge directions. Nobody knows what to count for "is this weld cracked?"

💡

Which is also the honest limit: if you have 200 images and a well-understood problem, a designed feature may still be the better engineering choice. Sub-topic E is about what to do when you only have 200.

lab_a.py💻 lab.ipynb — open in Colab
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_circles
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier

x, w, b = np.array([2., -1., 3.]), np.array([0.5, 2., -1.]), 0.5
print("one neuron:", max(0, w @ x + b))       # the whole definition

X, y = make_circles(500, noise=.07, factor=.45, random_state=3)
print("straight line ", LogisticRegression().fit(X, y).score(X, y))
print("8 hidden ReLU", MLPClassifier((8,), max_iter=4000,
                                    random_state=1).fit(X, y).score(X, y))

one neuron: 0.0 — the sum is −3.5, and ReLU clips it. Then straight line 0.5 and 8 hidden ReLU 1.0. Two lines of difference, and one of them cannot do the task at all. TODO: the neuron wakes at b > 4.0 · random_state=7 → 0.998.

explore_a.py
# TODO 1: run the sweep and note where the accuracy jumps.
# TODO 2: rerun it with noise=.15 in make_circles — does the jump move?
for h in [1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 64]:
    m = MLPClassifier((h,), max_iter=4000, random_state=1).fit(X, y)
    print(f"hidden={h:3d} | accuracy {m.score(X, y):.3f}")
🔎

Measured here: 0.500 · 0.642 · 0.824 · 0.998 · 1.000 · 1.000. One neuron is exactly chance, and the jump happens at four — which is the geometry: it takes at least four straight cuts to fence off a bounded region, and each ReLU unit is one cut. Then going from 8 to 64 buys nothing — capacity you do not need is not free, it is just unused, and in sub-topic E it becomes actively harmful. B · Convolution That Learns Its Kernel Key Terms — A Conv Layer

Kernel / filter

/ˈkɜː.nəl/

The small grid of weights slid over the image. In a CNN these are exactly the weights that training changes.

ตารางน้ำหนักเล็ก ๆ ที่เลื่อนทาบภาพ · ใน CNN คือตัวเลขที่การเทรนไปปรับ

Feature map

/ˈfiː.tʃər mæp/

The image that one kernel produces. One kernel in, one map out.

ภาพผลลัพธ์ของ kernel หนึ่งตัว · หนึ่ง kernel ได้หนึ่ง map

Channels

/ˈtʃæn.əlz/

How many maps a layer produces — and therefore how deep the next layer's input is. A colour photo starts at 3.

จำนวน map ที่ชั้นนั้นผลิต = ความลึกของ input ชั้นถัดไป · ภาพสีเริ่มที่ 3

Parameter sharing

/pəˈræm.ɪ.tər/

The same kernel is used at every position. An edge is an edge wherever it appears, so the weights are reused.

ใช้ kernel ตัวเดียวกันทุกตำแหน่ง · ขอบก็คือขอบไม่ว่าจะอยู่ตรงไหน จึงใช้น้ำหนักซ้ำได้

🔑

Only the first card is new, and even that is a change of where the numbers come from, not of what happens to them. The sliding, the multiplying and the summing are byte-for-byte what Session 2 did.

1 / 63
B · Convolution That Learns Its Kernel Give it examples instead of instructions, and it finds the same thing
🤯

Nobody wrote the word "edge" anywhere in that run. It saw an image and a desired output and adjusted nine numbers until the error stopped falling — and it arrived at Sobel's kernel from 1968, to two decimal places. That is the entire idea of a CNN, at the smallest possible scale.

1 / 63
B · Convolution That Learns Its Kernel A layer is not one kernel — it is a stack of them
🧱

Read the shapes out loud: 1 channel in → 6 kernels → 6 channels out. The next layer's kernels are therefore not 3×3, they are 3×3×6 — each one looks at all six maps at once. That third number is where beginners lose track, and it is the whole content of sub-topic C.

1 / 63
B · Convolution That Learns Its Kernel Sharing the same nine numbers everywhere is what makes this possible
♻️

268 million weights against nine. The saving comes from one assumption about images: a pattern worth detecting in the top-left corner is worth detecting in the bottom-right too, so the same detector can be reused everywhere. That assumption is true of photographs, which is why convolution works on images — and it is not true of, say, a spreadsheet, which is why nobody uses conv layers there.

1 / 63
B · Convolution That Learns Its Kernel 🌍 Use case: what the layers turn out to learn

First layer

Edges at various angles, blobs of colour, small gradients. Every network ever trained on photographs learns roughly this — including the nine numbers on slide 16.

Middle layers

Corners, textures, repeated motifs — combinations of the layer below. This is where a hand-designed pipeline would have stopped.

Deep layers

Parts of objects — a wheel, an eye, a letter shape. Nobody specified these; they are whatever reduced the loss.

🔬

This layered picture comes from visualising trained networks (Zeiler & Fergus 2014, and much since) — published work, not something this deck measured. What the deck did measure is the first rung of that ladder: slide 16's kernel is a first-layer edge detector, discovered rather than designed.

1 / 63
B · Convolution That Learns Its Kernel ↩ What if nobody had told you what to write?

Then you supply examples with answers instead, and gradient descent supplies the nine numbers. Slide 16 is that swap, carried out for real.

Notice what the swap costs you: you now need labelled data, and you no longer get to say why the kernel is what it is.

🧾

Which is a genuine trade, not a free upgrade — a Sobel kernel can be explained to a regulator; a learned one can only be tested. In medicine and safety work that difference decides the design.

B · Convolution That Learns Its Kernel 💻 LAB — Learn a 3×3 kernel yourself, in twelve lines
①Make the training pairs · ② run gradient descent · ③ compare with Sobel
lab_b.py💻 lab.ipynb — open in Colab
import numpy as np, cv2
img = cv2.imread(cv2.samples.findFile("building.jpg"), 0)
img = cv2.resize(img, (260, 179), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA).astype(np.float32)/255
sobel = np.array([[-1,0,1],[-2,0,2],[-1,0,1]], np.float32)
target = cv2.filter2D(img, -1, sobel).ravel()        # the answers
pad = np.pad(img, 1, mode="edge")                    # every 3x3 patch
P = np.stack([pad[i:i+img.shape[0], j:j+img.shape[1]]
              for i in range(3) for j in range(3)], -1).reshape(-1, 9)
w = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(scale=.05, size=9)   # start at random
for step in range(400):
    w -= 0.06 * (2/len(target)) * (P.T @ (P @ w - target))
print(np.round(w.reshape(3,3), 2))
# TODO 1: print the loss every 100 steps — is it still falling at step 400?
# TODO 2: divide w by np.abs(w).max() and compare it with sobel itself.
✅

Prints [[-1.02 -0.11 0.82] [-1.10 -0.03 1.10] [-0.76 0.14 0.98]] — negative on the left, near zero in the middle, positive on the right. Nine random numbers became an edge detector in 400 steps and no library. TODO: loss 0.311 → 0.026, still falling · normalised, w is Sobel's shape, not its numbers.

Two of them recover; one refuses to. Horizontal comes back cleanly, blur takes about 4,000 steps to settle near 0.11 everywhere, and identity after 400 steps is still a vague blob with 0.23 in the middle — it needs 40,000 steps to reach 0.99. Nothing is broken: neighbouring pixels look almost the same, so many different kernels produce almost the same output, and the loss barely changes along those directions. A flat loss surface is a slow one, and that is a real effect you will meet again on real models.

C · Reading an Architecture
C Sub-topic C · Reading an architecture — the shape it hands along, and where the weights sit
🌍 In the real world

Three conv layers hold 23,584 weights. One dense layer holds 131,200. Why?

1 / 63
C · Reading an Architecture Key Terms — The Four Knobs

Stride (S)

/straɪd/

How far the kernel jumps each step. Stride 2 skips every other position and halves the output.

ระยะกระโดดของ kernel · stride 2 = ข้ามทีละสอง output เหลือครึ่ง

Padding (P)

/ˈpæd.ɪŋ/

Extra border added before filtering, so the output can keep the input's size. Session 4's edge problem, solved the same way.

ขอบที่เติมเข้าไปก่อนกรอง เพื่อให้ขนาด output เท่าเดิม — เรื่องเดียวกับปัญหาขอบภาพในคาบ 4

Pooling

/ˈpuː.lɪŋ/

Shrink by keeping the maximum of each small block. No weights at all — it is a fixed rule.

ย่อภาพโดยเก็บค่าสูงสุดของแต่ละบล็อก · ไม่มีน้ำหนักให้เรียนเลย เป็นกฎตายตัว

Flatten & dense

/ˈflæt.ən/

Unroll the final maps into one long vector and connect every entry to every output. This is where the weights pile up.

คลี่ map ทั้งหมดเป็นเวกเตอร์ยาวเส้นเดียว แล้วต่อทุกช่องเข้าทุก output — จุดที่น้ำหนักไปกองกัน

👁

Nothing here is for an exam — there is no final exam. These four knobs are here so you can look at a network and see what it does to the picture: what shrinks, what grows, and where the weights collect.

1 / 63
C · Reading an Architecture What a CNN hands along — seen, not counted
📐

One formula sets every size: Wout​=(W−F+2P)/S+1. You will use F=3,P=1,S=1 nearly always — and that keeps the size unchanged, so the only sizes worth thinking about are the ones the pooling layers halve.

1 / 63
C · Reading an Architecture Pooling: smaller every time, and still recognisable
🔻

Pooling does two jobs at once. It cuts the amount of data by four each time, which is what keeps a deep network affordable — and it makes the answer slightly insensitive to where things are, since shifting a bright pixel by one usually leaves the block maximum unchanged. Look again at the blocks on the previous slide: the footprint shrinks while the depth grows. That is the standard shape of almost every CNN.

1 / 63
C · Reading an Architecture ↩ Why does one dense layer hold 84% of the weights?

Because a conv layer shares its kernel across all 64 positions, while a dense layer gives every input its own private weight to every output.

So the weights collect at the one place where sharing stops — right after Flatten, the red bar in the picture.

💡

And that is exactly why modern architectures pool aggressively before flattening, or replace the flatten with a global average over each map: shrink to 1×1×64 first and the same dense layer costs 8,320 instead of 131,200.

1 / 63
C · Reading an Architecture 💻 LAB — Watch the picture shrink, one stage at a time
lab_c.py💻 lab.ipynb — open in Colab
import cv2, numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

im = cv2.resize(cv2.imread(cv2.samples.findFile("building.jpg"), 0), (128, 128))
k = np.array([[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]], np.float32)

def pool(a):                                    # 2x2 max-pool, no weights
    h, w = a.shape[0]//2*2, a.shape[1]//2*2
    return a[:h, :w].reshape(h//2, 2, w//2, 2).max(axis=(1, 3))

s = im.astype(np.float32); plt.subplot(1, 4, 1).imshow(im, cmap="magma")
for i in range(3):                             # conv (padding kept), then pool
    s = pool(np.abs(cv2.filter2D(s, -1, k))); print("stage", i+1, s.shape)
    plt.subplot(1, 4, i+2).imshow(s, cmap="magma")
# TODO 1: also print s.size — how fast does the data itself shrink?
# TODO 2: which line is the conv, and which one is the pool?
✅

Each picture is a quarter of the last: 128 → 64 → 32 → 16 — the staircase from slide 26, on a real photograph. The windows are gone in the last one, but the bright band of facade and the dark band of grass survive in 256 numbers. TODO 1: 4096 → 1024 → 256, a quarter each time.

(c) It never shrinks — the last map still holds 16,384 numbers instead of 256, 64× more to carry into the dense layer. Pooling is not a detail; it is the budget.

D Sub-topic D · How it learns — a loss to minimise, one step at a time
🌍 In the real world

This is the number every training script prints. What is it, and what makes it fall?

1 / 63
D · How It Learns Key Terms — Training, in Four Words

Loss

/lɒs/

One number saying how wrong the model currently is. Training is nothing but making it smaller.

ตัวเลขตัวเดียวที่บอกว่าตอนนี้โมเดลผิดแค่ไหน · การเทรนคือการทำให้มันเล็กลง เท่านั้นเลย

Cross-entropy

/krɒsˈen.trə.pi/

The loss used for classification: it punishes being confident and wrong far more than being unsure.

loss สำหรับงานจำแนกประเภท · ลงโทษการ "มั่นใจแล้วผิด" หนักกว่าการ "ไม่แน่ใจ" มาก

Gradient

/ˈɡreɪ.di.ənt/

The slope of the loss with respect to one weight — which way, and how steeply, it goes downhill.

ความชันของ loss เทียบกับน้ำหนักหนึ่งตัว · บอกว่าทางลงอยู่ทิศไหนและชันแค่ไหน

Learning rate (η)

/ˈiː.tə/

How big a step to take downhill. The one setting you will change most often, and the easiest to get wrong.

ขนาดก้าวที่เดินลงเขา · เป็นค่าที่ปรับบ่อยที่สุด และตั้งผิดง่ายที่สุด

🔑

In one sentence: measure how wrong you are, find which way is downhill for every weight, take a small step that way, repeat. Optimisers, schedules and batch sizes are all refinements of that loop.

1 / 63
D · How It Learns w←w−η∂L/∂w — that is the whole algorithm
🏔️

Read the picture as the formula: the slope at the current point says which way, η says how far, the minus sign says downhill. Notice the steps get smaller near the bottom without anyone shrinking them — the slope itself flattens out. A real network does this for millions of weights at once, but each one obeys this same line.

1 / 63
D · How It Learns The step size decides whether you arrive at all
⚖️

Too small and you run out of patience before it arrives — after 40 steps it has crept from −2.60 only as far as 0.46, and the loss is still falling. Too large and each step overshoots further than the last: this run leaves the picture entirely. Both look like "the model is not learning", and they need opposite fixes, which is why reading the loss curve rather than the final number is the habit worth building.

1 / 63
D · How It Learns 🌍 Use case: reading a loss curve like a doctor reads a chart

Falls, then flattens

Healthy. Stop when the curve stops moving — more epochs after that only cost time and invite the problem in sub-topic E.

Falls very slowly

Usually η too small, or unscaled inputs. Try ten times the learning rate before you try a bigger model.

Jumps around, or NaN

η too large. Divide it by ten. A NaN loss is almost never a subtle bug — it is an overshoot.

Flat from step one

Something is disconnected: labels shuffled, no activation, or a learning rate of zero. Check the data before the model.

📈

Four shapes, four different fixes — and none of them is "add more layers". In practice you will spend far more time reading this curve than designing architectures, so plot it every single run, from the very first one.

1 / 63
D · How It Learns ↩ What is that number, and what makes it fall?

It is the loss — one number for how wrong the model is on the data it has just seen.

It falls because of step ③ and ④: for every weight, work out which direction reduces the loss, and nudge it that way. Nothing in the loop knows anything about images.

⚠️

And note the honest limit of that number: the loss only measures the examples the model was shown. Getting it to zero on those says nothing about anything else — which is exactly the trap in sub-topic E.

D · How It Learns 💻 LAB — Gradient descent in five lines
①Write a loss · ② write its slope · ③ loop, and watch w move
lab_d.py💻 lab.ipynb — open in Colab
loss  = lambda w: (w - 1.2)**2 + 0.4       # the bowl
slope = lambda w: 2*(w - 1.2)                # its derivative

w, eta = -2.6, 0.18
for step in range(41):
    if step % 10 == 0:
        print(f"step {step:3d} | w {w:7.3f} | loss {loss(w):7.3f}")
    w -= eta * slope(w)                     # the entire algorithm
# TODO 1: start from w = 5.0 instead of −2.6 — does it still arrive?
# TODO 2: set eta = 0.02 and look at step 40. How far did it get?
✅

w goes −2.600 → 1.156 → 1.199 → 1.200 → 1.200 and the loss 14.840 → 0.402 → 0.400 → 0.400. It is within 0.05 of the answer by step 10 and then just polishes. That is what "converged" looks like — and it is why a curve that is still visibly falling means you stopped too early. D · How It Learns 🔍 Explore — find the learning rate where it breaks
explore_d.py
# TODO 1: run the sweep and find where it stops converging.
# TODO 2: predict eta = 2.0 before you run it, then run it.
for eta in [0.02, 0.18, 0.5, 0.99, 1.0, 1.02]:
    w = -2.6
    for _ in range(40): w -= eta * slope(w)
    print(f"eta {eta:5.2f} -> w {w:12.4g}")
🔎

Measured: 0.02 → 0.458 (still crawling) · 0.18 → 1.200 · 0.5 → 1.200 · 0.99 → −0.494 (bouncing across the minimum, closing very slowly) · 1.0 → −2.600 — it lands back exactly where it started, every step, forever · 1.02 → −17.0 and growing. The edge is at exactly η=1 for this bowl: the update moves 2η times the distance to the minimum, so at η=1 you always arrive the same distance out on the far side. Real losses have no such clean threshold, which is why people search for the learning rate instead of deriving it. TODO 2: η = 2.0 reaches −4.6 × 10¹⁹ in 40 steps.

# A single neuron with no activation: pred = w * x, loss = (pred - y)**2
# Given w = 0.4, x = 2.0, y = 1.0, eta = 0.1
# TODO 1: compute pred and the loss by hand, then check in Python.
# TODO 2: dL/dw = 2*(w*x - y)*x. Compute it and do ONE update.
# TODO 3: loop 20 times and print w. What value does it approach, and
#         what is the loss there?
# TODO 4: one sentence — repeat with eta = 0.3 and say what changed and why.
✅

1 pred = 0.8, loss = 0.04. 2 dL/dw = 2(0.8−1.0)(2.0) = −0.8, so w goes up to 0.48 — the minus sign in the update turns a negative slope into an increase. 3 it approaches w = 0.5, where pred = 1.0 and the loss is 0. 4 at η=0.3 the steps overshoot and it diverges — with x = 2 the curvature is 8, so anything above η=0.25 is unstable. The safe learning rate depends on your data's scale, which is why people normalise inputs.

E · Making It Work on Your Data Key Terms — Small-Data Survival

Overfitting

/ˌəʊ.vəˈfɪt.ɪŋ/

Memorising the training set instead of learning the pattern. Visible as a gap between training and held-out scores.

จำข้อมูลฝึกแทนที่จะเรียนรูปแบบ · สังเกตจากช่องว่างระหว่างคะแนนชุดฝึกกับชุดที่ไม่เคยเห็น

Held-out / validation set

/vælɪˈdeɪ.ʃən/

Images the model never trains on. The only number that means anything.

ภาพที่ไม่เคยใช้ฝึกเลย · เป็นตัวเลขเดียวที่มีความหมายจริง

Augmentation

/ˌɔːɡ.menˈteɪ.ʃən/

Making more training images from the ones you have — as long as the transform does not change the right answer.

สร้างภาพฝึกเพิ่มจากภาพที่มี · ตราบใดที่การแปลงนั้นไม่ทำให้คำตอบเปลี่ยน

Transfer learning

/ˈtræns.fɜːr/

Starting from a model someone else trained on millions of images, and re-using its early layers.

เริ่มจากโมเดลที่คนอื่นเทรนด้วยภาพหลายล้านภาพ แล้วยืมชั้นต้น ๆ มาใช้

🎯

This is the sub-topic your project will actually depend on. Nobody in this room has a million labelled images — so the question is never "which architecture is best?", it is "what do I do with 300 photos?"

1 / 63
E · Making It Work on Your Data Free training images — until the transform changes the answer
🏷️

The first four teach the model something true: a 6 is still a 6 when it is tilted, cropped or dim. The last two teach it something false — a mirrored 6 is not a 6, and a 6 turned upside down is a 9. Which augmentations are safe is a question about your labels, not about your code, and no library can answer it for you. Horizontal flip is safe for cats and catastrophic for text.

1 / 63
E · Making It Work on Your Data The premise of transfer learning, checked
🔁

The first layer that gradient descent found on a building works on a box and on a handwritten digit — and it sits 0.964 cosine away from the Sobel kernel a person wrote in 1968. Early layers are not about your images; they are about images. That is exactly why you can download somebody else's first layers and keep them: they learned edges, and your problem also has edges.

1 / 63
E · Making It Work on Your Data Two questions decide what you do with a borrowed model
data similar to ImageNetdata very different
few images
(hundreds)		Freeze everything, train only the last layer. Lowest risk.Freeze the early layers, train the last few. Expect to work hard.
many images
(tens of thousands)		Fine-tune the whole model at a small learning rate.Fine-tune everything, or train from scratch if you have the compute.

Freeze = keep the borrowed weights fixed and train only a new head. Few parameters to fit, so few images needed.

Fine-tune = let the borrowed weights keep moving, slowly. More capacity, and more ways to overfit.

📚

The size of this effect on real images is published, not measured here — this deck has no GPU and no ImageNet weights. What it measured is the premise on the previous slide.

E · Making It Work on Your Data 🌍 The famous architectures are answers to problems, not magic names

AlexNet · 2012

Problem: can a CNN beat hand-designed features at all?
Answer: yes, given a GPU and a million images — and the field turned over in one year.

VGG · 2014

Problem: what shape should the layers be?
Answer: just stack 3×3 convs and pool — simple, regular, and still the mental model everyone uses.

ResNet · 2015

Problem: past ~20 layers, deeper models got worse — even on training data.
Answer: add a shortcut that skips each block, so a layer can learn to do nothing.

🧠

The ResNet story is the one worth carrying: the failure was not overfitting — the deeper model was worse at the data it had seen, which means the optimiser was failing, not the capacity. The shortcut made "output the input unchanged" easy to learn instead of hard. When you pick a pretrained backbone, ResNet is almost always the sane default.

1 / 63
E · Making It Work on Your Data ↩ 100% on its own training data. Would you ship it?

No. 100% on the training set is not a result, it is a warning — the model has enough capacity to memorise 60 images, so it did.

The fix is never "train longer". It is more data, augmentation, a borrowed backbone, or a smaller model — in that order of preference.

🚨

And the reporting rule that follows: never quote a number your model was trained on. If a report does not say which images were held out, the number in it means nothing.

lab_e.py💻 lab.ipynb — open in Colab
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3, random_state=0,
                                      stratify=y)
sc = StandardScaler().fit(Xtr); Xtr, Xte = sc.transform(Xtr), sc.transform(Xte)

for n in [60, 200, len(Xtr)]:
    m = MLPClassifier((256, 128), max_iter=600, random_state=0, alpha=1e-6)
    m.fit(Xtr[:n], ytr[:n])
    print(f"{n:5d} images | train {m.score(Xtr[:n], ytr[:n]):.3f}"
          f" | held-out {m.score(Xte, yte):.3f}")
# TODO 1: add n = 20 to the list. How big is the gap at 20 images?
# TODO 2: print the gap (train − held-out) next to each row.
✅

60 → train 1.000 | held-out 0.859 · 200 → 1.000 | 0.915 · 1257 → 1.000 | 0.978. The training score is 1.000 in every single case and tells you nothing at all. The gap — 14 points, then 8, then 2 — is the whole message. TODO: n = 20 → held-out 0.639, a 36-point gap.

# TODO 1-3: run all three sweeps below, one knob at a time
for a in [1e-4, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0, 30.0]:            # (a) weight decay
    ...
for h in [(8,), (16,), (64,), (256, 128)]:        # (b) model size
    ...
for it in [10, 40, 80, 600]:                     # (c) stop early
    ...
# TODO 4: report held-out accuracy for every setting
# TODO 5: one sentence — which knob helped most, and by how much?
🔎

This is the honest result, and it is not the one the textbook picture suggests. Baseline 0.859. Weight decay: 0.859 · 0.867 · 0.859 · 0.691 · 0.100 — the best setting bought less than one point, and too much collapsed the model to chance. Smaller models: 0.707 · 0.769 · 0.833 — every one of them worse. Early stopping: 0.689 · 0.846 · 0.859 — never better. So on this data, the three classic anti-overfitting knobs bought at most 0.8 points, while going from 60 to 1,257 images bought 12. Regularisation is damage control; data is the cure — and that ordering is the single most useful thing in this sub-topic.

Where you can use this 🌍 Three fields where "learn the features" changed the job

Every one of them had a hand-designed pipeline first, and every one of them replaced it:

🏭

Industrial inspection

The problem: is this weld, tile or solder joint defective?

Why learned wins: nobody can write down what "a bad weld" looks like, but a factory can label ten thousand photographs of them.

defect detection · PCB inspection · surface finish

🏥

Medical imaging

The problem: find the tumour, the fracture, the retinal lesion.

Why learned wins: the signal is subtle and the experts disagree — but the experts can still label. And this is where "held-out" stops being pedantic.

radiology · pathology · retinal screening

🌾

Agriculture & ecology

The problem: which plant, which pest, how ripe, how many.

Why learned wins: the variation — light, angle, season — is exactly what a descriptor cannot be written for, and exactly what augmentation is for.

crop disease · weed spraying · camera traps

Where you can use this 🌍 Turning this into your own project

a good topic = a few hundred images you can actually collect + a label you can defend + a held-out set you never touch

"Can it tell my two houseplants apart from a phone photo?"

100 photos each, varied light and angle · freeze a pretrained backbone, train the head · report held-out accuracy and show the failures.

"Which of these 3D prints came out wrong?"

Photograph good and bad prints on the same background · augment with rotation and brightness · compare against a Session-4 threshold baseline.

"Is the lecture-hall seat occupied?"

One fixed camera, frames labelled by hand · a small CNN is genuinely enough · report the confusion matrix, not one number.

📥

What a good report contains: how many images and how they were split · a held-out number, never a training one · the loss curve · and a baseline you beat — a Session-4 threshold or a HOG+SVM. A deep model that does not beat a simple baseline is a finding, and worth reporting honestly.

✎Quick Check — Same Layers, Three Budgets⏱ 3 min

All three networks below have exactly the same layers — three convs, three pools, two dense. Only the input size and what happens just before the dense layer differ. (a) Why does the middle one cost 3.5× more when no layer was added? (b) Which would you choose for a few hundred training photographs?

✅

(a) Doubling each side quadruples what reaches the flatten — 1024 numbers become 4096 — and every one of them gets its own weight into all 128 dense units. The three conv layers cost exactly the same in all three bars. (b) The orange one: 33,194 weights is already generous for a few hundred images, and global average pooling gets there without touching the input or the layers.

1 / 63
✎Quick Check — Why Is It Stuck at 50%?⏱ 3 min

A classmate's binary classifier is stuck at exactly 50% on a task where the two classes form two rings. Their model: Dense(256) → Dense(256) → Dense(1), no activations, trained for 5,000 epochs at a well-chosen learning rate. (a) What is wrong? (b) Why does the loss still go down at first? (c) What is the smallest fix?

✅

(a) No activations — three dense layers with nothing between them multiply out to one linear layer, and no straight line separates two rings. (b) It does go down, to the best a straight line can manage; it is converging correctly to a hopeless model. (c) Add ReLU after the first two layers — no new parameters, no new layers, one word. Note the diagnosis came from the shape of the task, not from the code.

1 / 63
🧮Worked Example — One Weight, One Step

Given

  • one weight, no activation: y^​=wx
  • w = 0.4 · x = 2.0 · y = 1.0
  • squared loss L=(y^​−y)2
  • η = 0.1

Find

  • the loss, the gradient, and w after one step
Predictŷ = 0.4 × 2.0 = 0.8
Loss(0.8 − 1.0)² = 0.04
Gradient2(ŷ − y)·x = 2(−0.2)(2.0) = −0.8
Updatew ← 0.4 − 0.1(−0.8) = 0.48
∴ w rose to 0.48 · repeat and it settles at 0.5, where the loss is 0
➖

Watch the two minus signs. A negative gradient means the weight must go up — the sign in the rule handles it, and getting it backwards is the classic first bug.

1 / 63
✎Quick Check — Which Augmentations Are Safe?⏱ 3 min

You are classifying road signs from dashcam photographs. For each transform, say whether it is safe, and in one clause say why.

✅

Safe: ② brightness (a sign at dusk is the same sign) · ③ small rotation (a slightly tilted camera) · ④ crop (framing varies) · ⑥ noise (cheap sensors are noisy). Unsafe: ① flip — "turn left" becomes "turn right", and mirrored text is not text · ⑤ 90° — no dashcam ever sees a sign on its side, so you are spending capacity on a case that never happens. The test is always: does the correct label survive, and does this actually occur in deployment?

📋The Case — 240 Photographs of Two Kinds of Bolt

The situation

  • A workshop wants to sort two bolt types automatically.
  • You have 240 photographs, 120 of each, taken on one bench.
  • Images are 128 × 128 colour.
  • The bolts are the same colour; they differ in head shape.
  • It must run on a laptop, and be finished in two weeks.

Answer these

  • Q1 — how do you split 240 images, and what must be true of the split?
  • Q2 — a 3-conv net like slide 26 on a 128×128 input: using the chart on slide 56, say what that does to the dense layer and name two ways to bring it back down.
  • Q3 — from scratch, freeze, or fine-tune? Justify from the two questions on slide 45.
  • Q4 — name the baseline you would beat before believing any of it.
💭

Work in order: split first — before you look at a single image — then size, then strategy, then baseline.

✔Part A — Answers
Q1Roughly 170 / 35 / 35 train / validation / test, stratified so both classes appear
in each. Critically: split before augmenting, or rotated copies of a training
image land in the test set and your score becomes fiction.
Q2Four times the area of a 64×64 input, so the flatten grows again — about
2.1 million weights in the dense layer alone, for 170 training images.
Shrink the input, add a pool, or use global average pooling — the orange bar.
Q3Freeze a pretrained backbone and train only the head. Few images, and bolts
are ordinary photographed objects — the top-left cell of the table.
Q4Something from Sessions 3–6: shape descriptors on the thresholded head, or
HOG + a linear SVM — the hook of this session says it will be competitive.
🧠

Q1 is the one that ruins real projects. Every leak — augmented copies, two photos of the same bolt, the same lighting session — inflates the number you report and nothing warns you. One bench and one lighting setup is itself a limitation: say so in the report.

💻Q5 — The First Experiment You Would Run

#         Re-measure. Did the gap narrow?
# TODO 5: one paragraph — report all three numbers, say which you would ship,
#         and state one thing your 240 bench photographs cannot tell you.
✅

Expected shape of the result: the baseline will be respectable, the from-scratch CNN will overfit visibly on 170 images, and augmentation will narrow the gap without closing it. The right answer to TODO 5 is frequently "ship the baseline" — and the thing 240 bench photographs cannot tell you is how any of them behaves on the factory floor, under different light, on a bolt neither of us has seen.
